title: Technology shares at a record
what: The Nasdaq index closed at a record 328.91 on 24 June, about 40% higher than at the start of the year. Computer and chip companies lead the rise: Intel gained about 30% in June alone. IBM has sold its PC far faster than it planned. The business behind the shares is growing fast: last year more than a hundred companies sold 2.8 million personal computers for 4.9 billion dollars. Apple's sales rose 74 percent to 583 million dollars, and Intel's reached a record 900 million.
why: The top of the 1983 high-tech boom. By July 1984 the Nasdaq was 32% lower as home computers turned into a price war.
source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NASDAQCOM (read 2026-10-03); data/out/intc.json (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_Personal_Computer (read 2026-10-03); https://www.islandnet.com/~kpolsson/comphist/comp1982.htm (search result read 2026-10-04); https://timeline.intel.com/1982/financial-year-1982 (search result read 2026-10-04); https://wallstreetnumbers.com/stocks/aapl/revenue (search result read 2026-10-04)
changed: note to the writer addressed: sales figures of 1982 added

title: Computer shares lead a January surge
what: The Nasdaq index rose 12% in January to 392, and computer companies rose far more: Microsoft about 52%, Intel 49% and Apple 37%. Personal computers built on Intel's new 386 chip, the first from Compaq since September, are on sale, and investors are betting on a recovery after the chip slump of 1985 and 1986.
why: The PC wave's second leg. The broad market's +13% month belongs to the general 1987 boom; this beat gives the tech side.

title: Technology shares lead the war rally, and the price of growth climbs
what: Technology shares led the January surge. Microsoft gained about 30% in the month and closed it at a new high after reporting bigger profits. Prudential-Bache cut the stock from buy to hold: it had risen almost 25% since mid-November and its price/earnings ratio was too high. At the new high Microsoft sells at about 42 times the earnings of its last fiscal year, which ended in June. Apple sells at about 15 times last year's earnings, helped by brisk sales of the cheap Macintosh Classic, and Intel at about 14 times its 1990 earnings, which rose to 650 million dollars. Analysts are split: Bear Stearns calls Apple a buy, Paine Webber calls it unattractive, and UBS Securities advises using the rally to sell technology stocks.
why: Company side of the Desert Storm month. In the game the growth names jumped about 30% while the S&P 500 rose 4% (Microsoft +30%, Cisco +30%, Apple +29%, LDDS +31%, Intel +19%; October 1990 to March 1991: Apple +121%, LDDS +97%, Microsoft +67%, Cisco +65%, S&P 500 +23%). The ratios show two different trades. Microsoft was already priced as a growth stock (about 42 times fiscal 1990 earnings, about 37 times the twelve months to September 1990), and the rally pushed it higher still. Apple and Intel were priced like ordinary industrials, at 14 to 15 times earnings, so their rise was a re-rating from the autumn panic lows. Arithmetic: Microsoft fiscal 1990 EPS 0.52 dollars as restated in the FY1994 10-K, times 4.5 to undo the 3-for-2 splits of 1991 and 1992 and the 2-for-1 split of 1994 named in the same filing = 2.34 dollars; 98.13 / 2.34 = 41.9. Twelve months to September 1990: 2.34 - 0.43 + 0.71 = 2.62 dollars (quarters from the Seattle Times, October 1990); 98.13 / 2.62 = 37.5. The pre-split basis checks out: 279 million dollars of fiscal 1990 net income / 2.34 = 119 million shares, against 123 million implied by the 71-cent quarter. Apple: 55.50 / 3.77 (fiscal year to September 1990, FY1994 10-K; no splits between 1987 and 2000) = 14.7. Intel: 45.75 / 3.20 (UPI) = 14.3. Prices are Computerworld's closing prices of 31 January 1991. Not sourced: Cisco and LDDS (neither in Computerworld's tables, no 1990-91 EPS found), the Nasdaq composite's January gain, and the figures of Microsoft's December quarter.
source: Computerworld, 4 February 1991, p. 90, 'Stocks' page: closing prices of 31 January 1991 (Microsoft 98.13, Apple 55.50, Intel 45.75), Bear Stearns and Paine Webber on Apple, https://archive.org/details/sim_computerworld_1991-02-04_25_5 (read 2026-10-17); Computerworld, 28 January 1991, 'Industry Almanac' and 'Stocks': Prudential-Bache downgrade of Microsoft, UBS Securities 'take advantage of the recent rally by selling technology stocks now', technology stocks 'continued to surge', Microsoft gaining on news of bigger profits to a new high, https://archive.org/details/sim_computerworld_1991-01-28_25_4 (read 2026-10-17); Microsoft Form 10-K for fiscal 1994, Exhibit 13 financial highlights (fiscal 1990 net income 279 million dollars, EPS 0.52 restated) and the note on the 3-for-2 splits of 1991 and 1992 and 2-for-1 split of 1994, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/789019/0000891020-94-000175.txt (read 2026-10-17); Seattle Times, 'Microsoft Profits Surge On Sales Of Windows 3.0', 16 October 1990 (71 cents against 43 cents a share), https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/19901016/1098536/microsoft-profits-surge-on-sales-of-windows-30 (read 2026-10-17); Seattle Times, 'Microsoft Stock And Gates' Worth Soar', 7 February 1991, https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/19910207/1264869/microsoft-stock-and-gates-worth-soar (read 2026-10-17); Apple Computer Form 10-K for fiscal 1994, selected financial data (fiscal 1990 EPS 3.77 dollars), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/0000320193-94-000016.txt (read 2026-10-17); UPI, 'Intel 1990 earnings rise, but analysts unimpressed', 17 January 1991, https://www.upi.com/Archives/1991/01/17/Intel-1990-earnings-rise-but-analysts-unimpressed/6143664088400/ (read 2026-10-17); price changes from data/out/msft.json, aapl.json, intc.json, csco.json, worldcom.json and sp500.json

title: The World Wide Web opens to the internet: there is one website
what: On 23 August Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web, a system of linked pages developed at the CERN physics laboratory in Geneva, was made available to the whole internet. The internet itself still links mainly universities and research labs. There is nothing to surf yet: no shops, no newspapers, no search engines, no pictures. The internet is a way for scientists to send each other messages and files, and almost nobody outside the universities has heard of it.
why: Nobody on Wall Street noticed. Four years later it was the foundation of the biggest stock mania since the 1920s.

title: Mosaic: a program that makes the internet something to look at
what: Two programmers at the University of Illinois, Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina, have written Mosaic, a 'browser' for the World Wide Web, and since September it also runs on ordinary Windows and Macintosh computers. It is the first that shows pictures and text together on one page, and to move from page to page a click of the mouse is enough. It is free and easy to install. There is not much to see so far: late last year the whole Web consisted of 26 sites.
why: The moment the internet leaves the universities: Mosaic is downloaded 50,000 times a month by mid-1994, Andreessen founds Netscape, and by August 1995 there are more than 10,000 websites.

title: Compaq passes IBM as the biggest PC maker
what: Compaq, which began by copying the IBM PC, sold more personal computers than IBM or Apple in 1994; in the US it had 12.6% of the market against Apple's 11.6%. In 1991 a price war had brought Compaq its first loss and its first layoffs.
why: The PC had become a commodity: the profits went to Intel's chips and Microsoft's software, not to the box makers. That is why IBM and Apple struggled in the 1990s while Intel and Microsoft soared.

title: Windows 95 launches with a billion-dollar campaign
what: Microsoft launched Windows 95 on 24 August, with the Rolling Stones' Start Me Up in its advertising and a marketing effort estimated at a billion dollars. One million copies shipped worldwide in the first four days. It has a Start button and a taskbar, and runs on Intel chips.
why: The PC wave's peak cultural moment; Windows 95 brought millions of new users online and made Microsoft the most powerful company in technology.

title: 16 million people are online. A fad, say the sceptics
what: At the end of 1995 about 16 million people in the world used the internet, less than half a percent of mankind. Not everybody believes it will matter. 'The Internet? Bah!' wrote the astronomer Clifford Stoll in Newsweek last February: no online database would replace the daily newspaper, and people would not shop over a computer. Robert Metcalfe, who invented the Ethernet network cable, predicts that the internet will collapse this year under its own growth, and has promised to eat his words if it does not.
why: The cautious beginning. Metcalfe did eat his column in 1997, mixed with water in a blender, in front of a conference audience.
source: https://www.stackscale.com/blog/internet-evolution-statistics/ (search result read 2026-10-04); https://www.allaboutmarketresearch.com/internet.htm (search result read 2026-10-04) (figures of Internet World Stats); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Stoll (read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Metcalfe (read 2026-10-04)

title: The internet more than doubles in a year: 36 million users
what: At the end of 1996 about 36 million people were online, against 16 million a year before. The collapse that the network pioneer Robert Metcalfe had predicted for 1996 did not happen. The World Wide Web, which consisted of 26 sites in late 1992, had passed 10,000 sites by the summer of 1995 and has kept growing ever since.
why: The growth becomes visible to everybody; the forecasts turn from doubt to enthusiasm.
source: https://www.stackscale.com/blog/internet-evolution-statistics/ (search result read 2026-10-04); https://www.allaboutmarketresearch.com/internet.htm (search result read 2026-10-04) (figures of Internet World Stats); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Metcalfe (read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosaic_(web_browser) (read 2026-10-04)

title: Faster than radio, faster than television: the internet reaches 70 million
what: It took radio 38 years to reach 50 million listeners and television 13 years to reach 50 million viewers. The internet did it in four, says a report the American government published on 15 April. At the end of 1997 about 70 million people were online, twice as many as a year before, and according to the report the traffic on the internet doubles every hundred days. Electronic commerce, it says, brings growth, well-paid jobs and lower inflation.
why: The official blessing of the boom. 'Doubling every hundred days' was true for a short time in 1995 and 1996 at most; telephone companies such as WorldCom nevertheless built networks for it, which is one reason for the telecom bust of 2001.
source: https://www.stackscale.com/blog/internet-evolution-statistics/ (search result read 2026-10-04); https://www.allaboutmarketresearch.com/internet.htm (search result read 2026-10-04) (figures of Internet World Stats); https://hannemyr.com/en/diff.html (search result read 2026-10-04); https://library.unt.edu/gpo/oca/mrapr98.htm (search result read 2026-10-04)

title: 147 million online, and a book called 'Dow 36,000'
what: At the start of this year 147 million people used the internet, again twice as many as the year before. The forecasts grow with it. A new book by James Glassman and Kevin Hassett, 'Dow 36,000', argues that shares are still far too cheap: the Dow Jones index of big American companies should stand about four times higher than today, at 36,000, within a few years.
why: The forecasts have gone from sceptical to wild. The Dow reached 36,000 in November 2021, twenty-two years later.
source: https://www.stackscale.com/blog/internet-evolution-statistics/ (search result read 2026-10-04); https://www.allaboutmarketresearch.com/internet.htm (search result read 2026-10-04) (figures of Internet World Stats); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dow_36,000 (read 2026-10-04)

title: Nearly ten million Americans now trade shares online
what: On 22 November the SEC, America's stock market regulator, reported that online brokerage accounts have almost tripled, from 3.7 million in 1997 to 9.7 million by the middle of 1999. More than half a million trades a day are now placed over the internet, against fewer than 100,000 in 1996, and online trades made up 15.9 percent of all share trades early this year. Some of the new investors are day traders who buy shares in the morning and sell them in the afternoon, often with borrowed money, and stories of people quitting their jobs to trade are common.
why: The gold-rush mood made visible: millions of amateurs crowded into technology and internet shares near the top, and many lost as fast as they had won once the Nasdaq turned in March 2000.
source: SEC special study 'On-Line Brokerage: Keeping Apace of Cyberspace', 22 November 1999, https://www.sec.gov/news/studies/cyberspace.htm (read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_trading (read 2026-10-04)

title: The Nasdaq ends 1999 up 86%, above 4,000
what: The Nasdaq closed above 4,000 for the first time on 29 December, less than two months after first passing 3,000 on 3 November. It rose 22% in December alone and 85.6% in 1999, against 19.5% for the S&P 500. Telecom, phone and internet names led: Sony rose 55% in December, Nokia 36%.
why: The best year in the index's history and the height of the mania; the next fifteen years would not see these levels again.

title: A web address sells for 7.5 million dollars; Swiss artists refuse to sell theirs
what: Web addresses have become prized: this year Marc Ostrofsky sold the name business.com for 7.5 million dollars, a record price for a domain name; he had paid 150,000 dollars for it in the mid-1990s. The Zurich art group etoy would not sell at all. The online toy shop eToys wanted etoy.com, which the artists had used since 1995, two years before etoys.com opened; when etoy turned down its offers it sued over its trademark, and on 29 November a Los Angeles court shut etoy.com down. eToys then offered cash and eToys shares worth about half a million dollars to settle, and etoy refused again. In December artists and internet activists answered with 'Toywar', an online campaign calling on people to boycott eToys and sell its shares, which have more than halved since the court order; on 29 December eToys said it would try to end the case, but etoy's lawyer called its conditions unacceptable.
why: The price of a web address at the top of the boom, and a Swiss story: etoy's refusal of eToys' money and the Toywar campaign. (The VA Linux first-day jump that this beat used to carry was dropped at the curator's wish.) The January 2000 outcome, eToys dropping the suit, is for a later beat if wanted.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Ostrofsky (read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business.com (read 2026-10-04); https://rtmark.com.theyesmen.org/more/etoynpr19991213.html (NPR Morning Edition, 13 December 1999: half a million dollars offered and rejected) (read 2026-10-17); https://static-files.rhizome.org/Q2029/more/articles/etoyamericanreporter19991217.html (The American Reporter, 28 December 1999: settlement offer in eToys shares worth more than $400,000, falling with the share price; eToys shares down more than 50% since 29 November) (read 2026-10-17); https://static-files.rhizome.org/Q2029/more/articles/etoywired19991230-a.html (Wired News, 30 December 1999: injunction of 29 November, eToys' offer to end the case, etoy's lawyer) (read 2026-10-17); https://www.mcspotlight.org/debate/multis/messages/1252.html (3 December 1999: earlier offers of tens of thousands of dollars, boycott and sell-the-shares call) (read 2026-10-17); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etoy (domain used since 1995, etoys.com from 1997) (read 2026-10-17); https://www.theartnewspaper.com/archive/etoy-take-manhattan (offers from $30,000 in September 1999 to $516,000 in cash and shares) (read 2026-10-17)

title: AOL, an internet company, agrees to buy Time Warner
what: On 10 January America Online, which brings more than 20 million customers onto the internet, announced that it will take over the media group Time Warner for about 165 billion dollars, paid in its own shares. Although Time Warner has far bigger revenues and assets, AOL's shareholders will own 55 percent of the combined company, because the stock market values AOL more highly. The deal shows how much buying power soaring internet shares have given their owners. AOL's own shares fell 26% in January.
why: The new economy buying the old with inflated paper, two months before the Nasdaq's top; the deal became a byword for the excesses of the bubble.
changed: consistency review of November 2026: the story carried AOL's -26% but never said the shares fell; one sentence added from the game's prices

title: New economy up, old economy down
what: The Nasdaq rose 19% in February to 4,697 while the S&P 500 of large established companies fell 2%. Chip, telecom and internet shares are bought, while old-economy favourites are sold: Nvidia rose 73% this month and Siemens 31%, while Coca-Cola and McDonald's fell about 15%. At the Super Bowl at the end of January, a record 17 dot-com companies advertised. About 248 million people were online at the end of 1999, fifteen times as many as four years earlier.
why: The last, steepest leg of the bubble, and the widest split between new and old economy shares.
source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NASDAQCOM (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot-com_bubble (read 2026-10-03); https://www.stackscale.com/blog/internet-evolution-statistics/ (search result read 2026-10-04); https://www.allaboutmarketresearch.com/internet.htm (search result read 2026-10-04) (figures of Internet World Stats)

title: The Nasdaq loses 25% in a week
what: The Nasdaq fell 8% on 3 April, the day a judge ruled that Microsoft broke antitrust law. On 14 April it fell 9.7%, ending a week in which it lost 25%. It ended April at 3,861, almost a quarter below its March record.
why: The bubble bursts. There were sharp rallies to come, but the March peak was the high for fifteen years.
changed: consistency review of November 2026: the Microsoft ruling was told twice in April 2000; the details are left to the Microsoft story

title: 'Maybe the music has stopped': the Nasdaq is down a third
what: The slide of technology shares goes on. On 23 May the Nasdaq index fell as low as 3,173, 37 percent below its record of 5,049 on 10 March. Apple lost a third of its value in May, eBay a fifth and Cisco 18 percent. A week earlier, on 16 May, the Fed had raised its interest rate by half a point to 6.5 percent to cool the economy. Even the most famous investors have been caught out. George Soros, whose Quantum Fund lost 19 percent this year on internet shares, said: 'Maybe I don't understand the market. Maybe the music has stopped, but people are still dancing.' His chief investor Stanley Druckenmiller resigned on 28 April: 'I overplayed my hand.' Julian Robertson, who refused to buy internet shares at all, had given up a month earlier and closed his Tiger funds.
why: The mood turns: after March the question is no longer how high, but whether it was a bubble all along. The professionals lost both ways, those who joined in late and those who stayed out too early. The Nasdaq still had three quarters of its fall ahead of it.
source: https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2000/may/23/markets-have-wild-ride/ (search result read 2026-10-04); https://www.cnn.com/TRANSCRIPTS/0005/16/bn.01.html (search result read 2026-10-04); https://money.cnn.com/2000/04/28/mutualfunds/soros/ (search result read 2026-10-04); https://www.safalniveshak.com/risks-of-speculating-during-rising-markets/ (search result read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Robertson (read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot-com_bubble (read 2026-10-04)
changed: New Economy storyline: new lead story for May 2000 requested by the curator; consistency review of November 2026: Apple's -32% (one of its twelve biggest months) had no story; the month's lead now names the worst hit, from the game's prices

title: The Nasdaq's worst month since 1987
what: The Nasdaq fell 23% in November to 2,598, half its March record and its worst month since October 1987. The sell-off has spread from internet start-ups such as Pets.com, which is shutting down nine months after its IPO, to the big chip, PC and telecom equipment companies. Gloomy profit reports and signs of slower growth sent the S&P 500 down 8% in the month to 1,314.95.
why: The second leg of the crash, when the internet sell-off spread to the big technology companies. The S&P 500's -8% month was driven by tech.
changed: consistency review of November 2026: the closing of Pets.com was told twice in November 2000 (and dated 7 November in one story, 9 November in the other); it now has its own story only

title: The telecom bust: network gear makers crash
what: The Nasdaq fell 22% in February to 2,152, its lowest since late 1998. Telephone companies, which have borrowed heavily to build fibre-optic and mobile networks and paid billions for mobile licences in Europe, are cutting orders, and the makers of their equipment warn of falling sales; WorldCom is laying off about 6,000 workers. Cisco lost more than a third in February, and the makers of optical parts for the networks fared worse. Disappointing company earnings sent the S&P 500 down 9% to 1,239.94, despite two Fed rate cuts in January. Nokia cut its first-quarter sales growth forecast and its estimate for world phone sales this year, and its shares lost 36% in February.
why: The telecom bubble, financed by more than 500 billion dollars mostly of debt since 1996, began to burst; telecom companies lost about 700 billion dollars of market value over two years. The S&P's -9% month is this sell-off. Cost cuts as revenue growth stalled; behind the scenes, the improper capitalisation of line costs started in 2001.
source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NASDAQCOM (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecoms_crash (read 2026-10-03); https://money.cnn.com/2001/02/22/markets/markets_newyork/ (read 2026-10-03); https://www.federalreserve.gov/fomc/minutes/20010320.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Federal_Open_Market_Committee_actions (read 2026-10-03); data/reference/sp500.json; https://money.cnn.com/2001/01/30/europe/nokia/ via web.archive.org (read 2026-10-03); https://money.cnn.com/2001/03/15/europe/nokia/ via web.archive.org (read 2026-10-03); https://www.foxnews.com/story/worldcom-timeline (Associated Press timeline, 8 August 2002; read 2026-10-03)
changed: consistency review of November 2026: WorldCom's one-sentence story on 6,000 job cuts folded in (with worldcom/7674e542)

title: The Nasdaq falls below 2,000
what: On 12 March the Nasdaq fell 6.3% to 1,923.38, its first close below 2,000 since 1998 and 62% under the record of a year ago. It ended March at 1,840. Cisco lost another third this month.
why: A year after the peak, most of the bubble's gains were gone; the low was still eighteen months away.

title: The Nasdaq falls 78% below its record, then rebounds
what: On 9 October the Nasdaq closed at 1,114.11, 78% below its March 2000 record; about 5 trillion dollars of market value has been lost since the record. From there it rose 13.5% by the end of October, led by technology shares. The S&P 500, which had closed at 785.28 on 7 October, its lowest since 1997, ended the month up 9% at 885.76 as better-than-expected profit reports from several big companies lifted shares.
why: The low of the dot-com bust, though nobody could know it then. The S&P's +9% month is the start of the recovery. Review 2026-10: 'The bottom' was hindsight.

title: The most battered shares bounce hardest
what: The Nasdaq rose another 11% in November to 1,479. The shares that had fallen furthest rebounded most: Nvidia rose 44%, Cisco a third.
why: A classic bear-market bottom pattern: the junk rallies first. December gave back much of it.

title: Google goes public
what: Google, the most used search engine, sold shares to the public on 19 August, raising 1.67 billion dollars and valuing the company at more than 23 billion.
why: The first great internet IPO after the bust, and proof that the web could make huge profits from advertising.
changed: rule on metrics: offer price removed from title and text; the valuation at the offer price (23 billion, Wikipedia) kept

title: Amazon starts renting out storage over the internet
what: On 14 March Amazon launched S3, a service that stores other companies' data on Amazon's computers for a fee, under the name Amazon Web Services.
why: The quiet start of cloud computing, which by 2025 earned Amazon 129 billion dollars a year in sales and made Microsoft's comeback. Review 2026-10: 'the cloud begins' was hindsight.

title: The App Store opens
what: Apple opened the App Store on 10 July with 500 programs, 125 of them free, that anyone can download to an iPhone. There were 10 million downloads in the first weekend. Outside developers write the programs, and Apple takes a share of the sales.
why: Apps turned the smartphone into a platform, the way Windows had made the PC one; Nokia's Symbian never caught up.

title: The first Android phone
what: On 23 September T-Mobile announced the G1, made by HTC, the first phone using Android, Google's free operating system for phones. It will cost 179 dollars with a two-year contract from 20 October.
why: Android gave every other phone maker an answer to the iPhone and left Nokia squeezed between Apple at the top and cheap Android phones below.

title: The iPad sells 300,000 on its first day
what: Apple's iPad, a tablet computer announced on 27 January at 499 dollars, went on sale in the US on 3 April and sold 300,000 units the first day. Apple is selling a whole family of touch-screen devices running the same apps.
why: The mobile wave reached the PC's territory; PC sales and Intel's business with them stagnated in the following years.

title: Facebook's IPO disappoints
what: Facebook, the social network, went public on 18 May, raising 16 billion dollars and valuing it at 104 billion, the highest ever for a newly listed company. Technical problems at Nasdaq delayed trading, and the shares closed the first day barely above the offer price. By the end of May they were more than a quarter below it.
why: Social media's coming of age on the stock market; the shares bottomed below 18 in September.
changed: rule on metrics: IPO price and closes replaced by changes against the offer price (38 to 38.23; below 28)

title: The Nasdaq above its 2000 record, fifteen years on
what: On 23 April the Nasdaq closed at 5,056.06, above its record of 10 March 2000 for the first time. It had first returned above 5,000 on 2 March. Unlike in 2000, today's largest technology companies earn large profits.
why: The full round trip of the dot-com bust took fifteen years, a lesson in what buying at the top of a mania costs.

title: A computer beats one of the world's best Go players
what: Go is an ancient board game from Asia and far harder for computers than chess: until last year the best programs played like amateurs. From 9 to 15 March in Seoul, AlphaGo, a program built by Google's DeepMind, beat Lee Sedol, one of the best players in the world, by 4 games to 1. In the second game it played a move that professionals called creative, one that most of them would never have considered. About 60 million people watched in China alone.
why: An early sign of what artificial intelligence can do, six years before ChatGPT: the build-up to the Age of AI. An early sign of the artificial-intelligence wave; the learning methods behind it run on the graphics chips that made Nvidia the AI boom's winner.
changed: consistency review of November 2026: AlphaGo's win was told twice in March 2016; the fuller story is kept (with tech/44a0d949)

title: Four technology giants report on one evening; Amazon jumps 13% in a day
what: After the market closed on 26 October, Amazon, Microsoft, Google's parent Alphabet and Intel all reported results that pleased investors. Amazon's sales rose 34% to 43.7 billion dollars, and those of its cloud business, which rents out computing power, 42%; Microsoft's sales rose 12% to 24.5 billion, with its Azure cloud up 90%; Intel earned 4.5 billion dollars and raised its forecast for the year. The next day Amazon rose 13.2%, Intel 7.4%, Microsoft 6.4% and Alphabet 4.3%, adding 146 billion dollars to their combined value, more than all of IBM is worth, and the Nasdaq index rose 2.2% to a record 6,701. Over October Intel gained 19%, Amazon 15% and Microsoft 12%.
why: The day the market understood how much money the cloud makes, and a marker of the concentration of the index in a handful of technology companies that shapes the years after. Explains three of the month's biggest moves.

title: Stuck at home, the world goes online: Nasdaq above 10,000
what: The Nasdaq closed above 10,000 for the first time on 10 June, less than three months after falling to 6,861 on 23 March in the pandemic crash. With offices, shops and schools closed, people work, shop and learn online, and the largest technology companies have gained most.
why: The pandemic pulled forward years of digital adoption and began the 2020-21 tech boom.

title: OpenAI releases ChatGPT
what: On 30 November OpenAI, a San Francisco research company in which Microsoft invested a billion dollars in 2019, released ChatGPT, a program that answers questions and writes texts in ordinary language. It is free to use. It runs in Microsoft's Azure data centres on thousands of Nvidia graphics processors.
why: The start of the AI wave: it reached a million users in five days and 100 million within two months, the fastest-growing application then known, and set off the Nvidia-led boom.

title: Korea's chip crash
what: South Korea's stock market crashed in July, the KOSPI index losing more than 40% in about 40 days as investors sold Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the memory-chip makers that make up more than half of it. The fear is that big technology companies, which have not yet earned back their AI spending, will order fewer high-bandwidth memory chips.
why: The first serious break in the AI chip trade; Intel fell 35% and Nokia 31% in July while the broad US market held steady.
